title: What It Is to Know God — Tendency of This Knowledge
sectionSummaries: 1. The knowledge of God the Creator defined. The substance of this knowledge, and the use to be made of it.

2. Further illustration of the use, together with a necessary reproof of vain curiosity, and refutation of the Epicureans. The character of God as it appears to the pious mind, contrasted with the absurd views of the Epicureans. Religion defined.

paragraphs: By the knowledge of God, I understand that by which we not only conceive that there is some God, but also apprehend what it is for our interest, and conducive to his glory, what, in short, it is befitting to know concerning him. For, properly speaking, we cannot say that God is known where there is no religion or piety. I am not now referring to that species of knowledge by which men, in themselves lost and under curse, apprehend God as a Redeemer in Christ the Mediator. I speak only of that simple and primitive knowledge, to which the mere course of nature would have conducted us, had Adam stood upright. For although no man will now, in the present ruin of the human race, perceive God to be either a father, or the author of salvation, or propitious in any respect, until Christ interpose to make our peace; still it is one thing to perceive that God our Maker supports us by his power, rules us by his providence, fosters us by his goodness, and visits us with all kinds of blessings, and another thing to embrace the grace of reconciliation offered to us in Christ. Since, then, the Lord first appears, as well in the creation of the world as in the general doctrine of Scripture, simply as a Creator, and afterwards as a Redeemer in Christ,—a twofold knowledge of him hence arises: of these the former is now to be considered, the latter will afterwards follow in its order. But although our mind cannot conceive of God, without rendering some worship to him, it will not, however, be sufficient simply to hold that he is the only being whom all ought to worship and adore, unless we are also persuaded that he is the fountain of all goodness, and that we must seek everything in him, and in none but him. My meaning is: we must be persuaded not only that as he once formed the world, so he sustains it by his boundless power, governs it by his wisdom, preserves it by his goodness, in particular, rules the human race with justice and Judgment, bears with them in mercy, shields them by his protection; but also that not a particle of light, or wisdom, or justice, or power, or rectitude, or genuine truth, will anywhere be found, which does not flow from him, and of which he is not the cause; in this way we must learn to expect and ask all things from him, and thankfully ascribe to him whatever we receive. For this sense of the divine perfections is the proper master to teach us piety, out of which religion springs. By piety I mean that union of reverence and love to God which the knowledge of his benefits inspires. For, until men feel that they owe everything to God, that they are cherished by his paternal care, and that he is the author of all their blessings, so that nought is to be looked for away from him, they will never submit to him in voluntary obedience; nay, unless they place their entire happiness in him, they will never yield up their whole selves to him in truth and sincerity.

Those, therefore, who, in considering this question, propose to inquire what the essence of God is, only delude us with frigid speculations,—it being much more our interest to know what kind of being God is, and what things are agreeable to his nature. For, of what use is it to join Epicures in acknowledging some God who has cast off the care of the world, and only delights himself in ease? What avails it, in short, to know a God with whom we have nothing to do? The effect of our knowledge rather ought to be, first , to teach us reverence and fear; and, secondly , to induce us, under its guidance and teaching, to ask every good thing from him, and, when it is received, ascribe it to him. For how can the idea of God enter your mind without instantly giving rise to the thought, that since you are his workmanship, you are bound, by the very law of creation, to submit to his authority?—that your life is due to him?—that whatever you do ought to have reference to him? If so, it undoubtedly follows that your life is sadly corrupted, if it is not framed in obedience to him, since his will ought to be the law of our lives. On the other hand, your idea of his nature is not clear unless you acknowledge him to be the origin and fountain of all goodness. Hence would arise both confidence in him, and a desire of cleaving to him, did not the depravity of the human mind lead it away from the proper course of investigation.

For, first of all, the pious mind does not devise for itself any kind of God, but looks alone to the one true God; nor does it feign for him any character it pleases, but is contented to have him in the character in which he manifests himself always guarding, with the utmost diligences against transgressing his will, and wandering, with daring presumptions from the right path. He by whom God is thus known perceiving how he governs all things, confides in him as his guardian and protector, and casts himself entirely upon his faithfulness,—perceiving him to be the source of every blessing, if he is in any strait or feels any want, he instantly recurs to his protection and trusts to his aid,—persuaded that he is good and merciful, he reclines upon him with sure confidence, and doubts not that, in the divine clemency, a remedy will be provided for his every time of need,—acknowledging him as his Father and his Lord he considers himself bound to have respect to his authority in all things, to reverence his majesty, aim at the advancement of his glory, and obey his commands,—regarding him as a just judge, armed with severity to punish crimes, he keeps the Judgment-seat always in his view. Standing in awe of it, he curbs himself, and fears to provoke his anger. Nevertheless, he is not so terrified by an apprehension of Judgment as to wish he could withdraw himself, even if the means of escape lay before him; nay, he embraces him not less as the avenger of wickedness than as the rewarder of the righteous; because he perceives that it equally appertains to his glory to store up punishment for the one, and eternal life for the other. Besides, it is not the mere fear of punishment that restrains him from sin. Loving and revering God as his father, honouring and obeying him as his master, although there were no hell, he would revolt at the very idea of offending him.

Such is pure and genuine religion, namely, confidence in God coupled with serious fear—fear, which both includes in it willing reverence, and brings along with it such legitimate worship as is prescribed by the law. And it ought to be more carefully considered that all men promiscuously do homage to God, but very few truly reverence him. On all hands there is abundance of ostentatious ceremonies, but sincerity of heart is rare.

application: To know God, Calvin insists, is not to settle whether some deity exists but to apprehend him as the fountain of every good thing, and so to render him reverence and love — that union he calls piety, the root from which true religion springs. A God we merely concede but do not trust, fear, and obey is the idle God of Epicurus, with whom we have nothing to do. Our age is thick with that bargain: a vague higher power kept at a polite distance, ceremony without surrender, ostentation without sincerity of heart. Calvin's warning lands squarely on us — all do homage, few truly reverence. The remedy is not louder worship but a heart persuaded that it owes everything to its Father, and would shrink from offending him though there were no hell to fear. Build a household where God is sought as the source of every blessing, not consulted as a last resort. That is the difference between a Christian home and a religious one.

paragraphs: By the knowledge of God I mean the kind of knowledge by which we not only grasp that some God exists, but also understand what is good for us to know about him and what gives him glory — in short, what it is fitting for us to know concerning him. For strictly speaking, we cannot say that God is truly known where there is no religion or godliness. I am not speaking here of that kind of knowledge by which fallen and condemned people lay hold of God as their Redeemer in Christ the Mediator. I am speaking only of that plain and original knowledge to which the simple course of nature would have led us, had Adam never fallen.

It is true that now, in the present ruin of the human race, no one will see God as a Father, or as the author of salvation, or as favorable in any way, until Christ steps in to make our peace. Even so, it is one thing to recognize that God our Maker upholds us by his power, governs us by his providence, nourishes us by his goodness, and visits us with every kind of blessing — and quite another thing to embrace the grace of reconciliation offered to us in Christ. Since, then, the Lord first appears — both in the creation of the world and in the general teaching of Scripture — simply as a Creator, and afterward as a Redeemer in Christ, a twofold knowledge of him arises. The first of these is what we now have to consider; the second will follow afterward in its place.

Now although our mind cannot conceive of God without offering him some worship, it is still not enough simply to hold that he is the only being whom all ought to worship and adore. We must also be persuaded that he is the fountain of all goodness, and that we must seek everything in him, and in no one but him. What I mean is this: we must be persuaded not only that, just as he once formed the world, so he sustains it by his boundless power, governs it by his wisdom, preserves it by his goodness — and in particular rules the human race with justice and judgment, bears with us in mercy, and shields us by his protection. We must also be persuaded that not a single particle of light, or wisdom, or justice, or power, or uprightness, or genuine truth will be found anywhere that does not flow from him and of which he is not the cause. In this way we must learn to expect and ask all things from him, and to give thanks to him for whatever we receive.

For this sense of God's perfections is the true teacher of godliness, and out of godliness religion springs. By godliness I mean that union of reverence and love toward God which the knowledge of his benefits inspires. For until people feel that they owe everything to God, that they are cherished by his fatherly care, and that he is the author of all their blessings — so that nothing is to be sought apart from him — they will never submit to him in willing obedience. Indeed, unless they ground all their happiness in him, they will never give themselves up to him truly and wholeheartedly.

Those, then, who in studying this question set out to inquire what the essence of God is only mislead us with cold speculations. It is far more in our interest to know what kind of being God is, and what is consistent with his nature. For what good is it to join the followers of Epicurus in acknowledging some God who has thrown off all care for the world and only takes pleasure in his own ease? What is the use, in short, of knowing a God with whom we have nothing to do? The effect of knowing him ought to be, first, to teach us reverence and fear; and second, to lead us, under his guidance and teaching, to ask every good thing from him, and, when we receive it, to credit it to him.

For how can the thought of God enter your mind without at once giving rise to this thought as well: that since you are his handiwork, you are bound by the very law of creation to submit to his authority — that your life is owed to him, and that whatever you do should have reference to him? If this is so, it certainly follows that your life is badly corrupted if it is not shaped in obedience to him, since his will ought to be the law of our lives. On the other hand, your idea of his nature is not clear unless you acknowledge him to be the origin and fountain of all goodness. From this would arise both trust in him and a longing to cling to him — if only the corruption of the human mind did not pull it away from the right course of inquiry.

For first of all, the godly mind does not invent for itself some God of its own, but looks to the one true God alone. Nor does it make up for him any character it pleases, but is content to take him as he reveals himself, always guarding with the utmost care against overstepping his will and wandering, by reckless presumption, from the right path. The person who knows God in this way sees how he governs all things, and so trusts him as his guardian and protector and casts himself entirely on his faithfulness. Seeing that he is the source of every blessing, the moment he is in any difficulty or feels any need, he turns at once to his protection and relies on his help. Persuaded that he is good and merciful, he rests on him with sure confidence, and does not doubt that the divine kindness will provide a remedy for his every time of need.

Acknowledging him as his Father and his Lord, he counts himself bound to respect his authority in all things, to reverence his majesty, to aim at advancing his glory, and to obey his commands. Regarding him as a just judge, armed with severity to punish wrongdoing, he keeps the judgment seat always before his eyes. Standing in awe of it, he restrains himself and is afraid to provoke God's anger. Yet he is not so terrified by the thought of judgment that he would wish to slip away from God, even if a way of escape lay open before him. On the contrary, he embraces him no less as the avenger of wickedness than as the rewarder of the righteous, because he sees that it belongs equally to God's glory to store up punishment for the one and eternal life for the other. What is more, it is not merely the fear of punishment that holds him back from sin. Loving and revering God as his Father, honoring and obeying him as his Master, he would recoil at the very thought of offending him even if there were no hell at all.

This is what pure and genuine religion is: confidence in God joined with serious fear — a fear that includes within it willing reverence, and that brings with it the kind of true worship that the law prescribes. And we ought to weigh more carefully the fact that all people alike pay God outward homage, but very few truly reverence him. On every side there is an abundance of showy ceremonies, but sincerity of heart is rare.
